html:
Sorghum is a tall cereal grass that was domesticated from a wild African grass in the eastern Sudan, around 3000 BCE or earlier. It is now the world's fifth most important cereal crop.

It grows where wheat and rice struggle. It tolerates heat and drought and does well on poor soils, which made it a staple grain across the dry savannas of Africa. Along with pearl millet and African rice, it was one of the crops African farmers tamed on their own, apart from the farming of the Near East.

How it spread:

  • Across the Sahel and down into East and southern Africa, carried by farmers and herders, and in the south by Bantu-speaking peoples of the Bantu expansion.
  • East across the Arabian Sea to India, by the second millennium BCE, along with other African millets. In India it is called jowar.
  • Later to China, where it is used to make strong liquors.
  • To the Americas with the Atlantic slave trade, later becoming a feed crop on the American plains.

People eat it as porridge, flatbread and couscous, and brew it into beer, which in much of Africa is part of social and ritual life. Its stalks feed animals and roof houses, and one variety is made into brooms. Today it feeds hundreds of millions of people in Africa and South Asia, and it is also grown for animal feed and ethanol. Its early history ties into the river states of Nubia, whose farmers lived in the region where it was first grown.
sum: Sorghum is a tall cereal grass that was domesticated from a wild African grass in the eastern Sudan, around 3000 BCE or earlier. It is now the world's fifth most important cereal crop.
